2003 saw many sequels and prequels in video games, such as Tony Hawk's Underground, Madden NFL 2004, NBA Live 2004, ESPN NBA Basketball, Saya no Uta: The Song of Saya, Final Fantasy X-2, Mario Kart: Double Dash, Mario & Luigi: Superstar Saga, Prince of Persia: The Sands of Time, Sonic Heroes, Postal 2, Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic, Uru: Ages Beyond Myst, and WWE SmackDown! Here Comes the Pain.

New intellectual properties included Beyond Good & Evil, Boktai: The Sun is in Your Hand, Call of Duty, Disgaea, Drakengard, Manhunt, PlanetSide, TrackMania, True Crime: Streets of LA, and Viewtiful Joe. The year's best-selling video game worldwide was Pokémon Ruby/Sapphire, the fifth time a Pokémon games was the annual worldwide top-seller (since 1998).

Financial performance

[edit]

Computer games continue to lose ground to console video games with a US sales drop of 14% in 2003.[1] Total 2003 entertainment software sales in the United States grew slightly to US$7 billion; console sales increased to $5.8 billion and computer games accounted for the remaining $1.2 billion.[2]

Major events

[edit]
Date Event Ref.
February 19 Microsoft announces a deal to buy Connectix Corporation. [citation needed]
February 27 Academy of Interactive Arts & Sciences hosts 6th Annual Interactive Achievement Awards; inducts Yu Suzuki of Sega to the AIAS Hall of Fame. [citation needed]
March 6–9 Game Developers Conference hosts 3rd annual Game Developers Choice Awards and Gama Network's 5th annual Independent Games Festival (IGF). [citation needed]
March 23 Nintendo stops production of the original Game Boy and Game Boy Color worldwide. [citation needed]
April 1 Enix Corporation and Square Co., Ltd. officially merge, forming Square Enix Co., Ltd. [citation needed]
April Pan European Game Information (PEGI), a European video game content rating system, comes into use. [citation needed]
May 7 Infogrames Entertainment, SA rebrands all its subsidiaries under the Atari brand. [citation needed]
May 14–16 9th annual E3 (Electronic Entertainment Expo) held at Los Angeles Convention Center; 6th annual Game Critics Awards for the Best of E3. [32]
May The 3DO Company announces bankruptcy and closes down its New World Computing subsidiary. [citation needed]
June 12 Obsidian Entertainment founded. [citation needed]
July 16 Interactive Digital Software Association (IDSA) renamed as Entertainment Software Association (ESA). [citation needed]
July IEMA (Interactive Entertainment Merchants Association) hosts 4th annual Executive Summit. [citation needed]
August 1 Virgin Interactive is renamed to Avalon Interactive by its owner Titus Software. [citation needed]
August Microsoft announced ATI as the developer of the GPU for their next generation console, Project Xenon. Their previous contract with Nvidia was finished but the GPU of the Xbox continued in production. [citation needed]
September 12 Valve releases their game distribution software Steam out of beta. [citation needed]
September 23 Nintendo stops production of the Family Computer and Super Famicom in Japan. [33]
September Silicon Dreams Studio goes defunct. [citation needed]
October 1 DreamWorks SKG and Tecmo announce a movie adaptation of the video game Fatal Frame has been fast-tracked with John Rogers and Steven Spielberg's involvement. [citation needed]
October 12–18 The 2003 World Cyber Games are held. [34][35]
October 20 Families of Aaron Hamel and Kimberly Bede, two young adults shot by teens William and Josh Buckner (who in statements to investigators claimed their actions were inspired by Grand Theft Auto III), file a US$246 million lawsuit against developer Rockstar Games, publisher Take-Two Interactive, retailer Walmart, and console-maker Sony. [citation needed]
October 31 British Academy of Film and Television Arts announces that nominations for the 6th annual BAFTA Interactive Entertainment Awards will instead be split between the 1st annual BAFTA Games Awards for video game publications and (on November 24) the BAFTA Interactive Awards for multimedia technologies; ceremonies to be held in February 2004. [citation needed]
November Kazushige Nojima resigns from Square Enix. [citation needed]
December 2 The inaugural Spike Video Game Awards are held. [36]
December Interplay closes its Black Isle Studios division. [citation needed]
Unknown First PlayStation Portable prototype shown by Sony. [citation needed]
Unknown Nintendo states that its next generation console would be fully compatible with the GameCube. [citation needed]
Unknown Compile goes defunct. [citation needed]
Unknown Take-Two Interactive buys TDK Mediactive, Inc. [citation needed]
Unknown CNN Money reports that video games are a US$10 billion industry [citation needed]
Unknown Nintendo buys shares from Japanese toy and animation conglomerate Bandai making Nintendo one of Bandai's top 10 shareholders. [citation needed]
Unknown Data East goes defunct. [citation needed]

Hardware releases

[edit]

Nintendo released the Game Boy Advance SP, the second & declared as the definitive model of the Game Boy Advance (it's also been declared as the best entry in the Game Boy family overall). The GBA SP was the first handheld Nintendo console to have a rechargeable battery powered by an AC Adapter instead of using AA batteries.
